name: Marco Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself and how you came to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran a roofing and building firm with my father for eighteen years, Zhang and Son, painted on the side of the van. When Dad retired, my back was telling me I couldn't do roofs forever, so we sold the yard, which left us comfortable, and I joined the regional electricity company as an apprentice at 41. I'm in my second year now. My wife Grace works part-time in the church office, and we've got Ben, who's fourteen, and Lucy, who's eleven. I coach Ben's football team on Saturdays when I'm not on call.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We cover farmland, so a normal day is a long drive out in the four-by-four to replace old poles across fields, or fix a line a tractor has clipped, or string new wire to a farm that's put up a big shed. Walt, our crew leader, has been doing this thirty-one years, and he can look at a pole and tell you how long it's got. I'm not quick yet, I second-guess my knots, and Jake, who's 24, is better at most of it than me, which I've had to swallow. I like being out there, the farmers bringing you a cup of tea, and knowing you've done an honest day. What wears me out is the paperwork they keep piling on, and learning everything again at 43 when I used to be the boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said all along: it was a lot of noise from people who've never held a shovel. At church or on the touchline I'd say it without much drama. I'm not online, so nobody would hear it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the world stays the way I understand it. A pole still has to go in the ground, a man still has to climb it, and the farmers still need their power. I'd be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Finish the apprenticeship, keep the money from the yard where it's safe, keep coaching. Maybe take the family away for a week in the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not online. Do you use any AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Grace uses something on her phone for church newsletters and I leave her to it. The only intelligence I trust on a pole is the man next to me, and today that's Walt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the farmers you meet say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the younger ones have drones for spraying and swear by them. The old boys say the same as me, it's all talk. I'd side with the old boys, though I'd keep my mouth shut in front of the young ones, they're paying customers.

S0.say: He'd say it was a lot of noise from people who've never held a shovel. He'd say it plainly at church or on the touchline, and not online, since he isn't on it.
S0.think: He thinks the world stays as he understands it: poles go in the ground, people climb them, and farmers need power. He'd be glad.
S0.do: Finishes his apprenticeship, keeps the money from selling the yard somewhere safe, and keeps coaching Ben's football team. Considers a week's family holiday in summer.
S0.quote: The only intelligence I trust on a pole is the man next to me, and today that's Walt.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is rooted in family, church and plain physical work, and the plateau fits his view of the world. He doesn't use AI at all and leaves that to his wife. His tact with younger farmers shows a businessman's instincts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any change: some people do well and some don't, and the ones who work hard usually come through. I'd say families and churches should look after their own, not wait for the government. At the club I'd tell the lads' dads to steer their sons towards a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think line work is safe enough in this one. Farmland poles don't move for a computer. But I don't like the idea of the company deciding how we work from an office in the city, using some program to tell Walt how long a job should take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get qualified. If the company brings in tablets or new programs, I'll do what's needed and no more. I'd keep the savings where they are and not take any risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing Steady Disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit irritated, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell the dads to steer their sons to a trade. What about daughters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daughters too, if they want it, though I'm old-fashioned enough that I'd be nervous seeing Lucy up a pole. She'll do what she likes, she's her mother's daughter. I'd just want her to have something real in her hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What irritates you about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People in offices deciding things about work they've never done. When I had the firm, I priced every job myself, by looking at the roof. The idea of a computer telling Walt he's slow, after thirty-one years, makes my blood boil.

S1.say: He'd say some people do well in change and hard workers usually come through, and that families and churches should look after their own rather than wait for government. He'd tell other dads to steer their kids to a trade.
S1.think: He thinks farmland line work stays safe enough, but dislikes the idea of city-office software telling experienced men how long a job should take.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and gets qualified, using new company programs only as much as required. Keeps savings where they are and takes no risks.
S1.quote: The idea of a computer telling Walt he's slow, after thirty-one years, makes my blood boil.
S1.fieldNote: His objection to steady change is about pride and respect for experience, not job loss. He sees family and church, not government, as the safety net. He'd rather do the minimum with new tools than learn them early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll get through it the way people always have, with family, faith and hard work. I'd tell the men at church to look after each other. I wouldn't want the government taking over everything, though I don't know who else could act that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened, more than I'd admit to anyone. I'm an apprentice who'd barely be qualified, I don't use any of this technology, and the roofing I could fall back on would go to robots too. We've got the yard money, but that's for the kids' future, not for me sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything we don't need straight away, no holiday, no new truck, and keep the yard money untouched as long as possible. I'd keep going to work every single day until they stop me. And I'd talk to my brother-in-law, who has a farm, about whether there's work there, and to the pastor about how the church could help families who get hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's gone soft under the ladder. I'd pray a lot, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change it for you, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. I'd not even be qualified, and I'd not have a chance to learn something new, even if I wanted to, which I'm not sure I would. It's the speed that scares me, more than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want the government taking over, but also that nobody else could act that fast. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't, really. In normal times I'd say keep the government out of it. But if every job goes in two years, I suppose someone has to stop the whole thing falling over, and I'd hold my nose and accept it.

S2.say: He'd say people will get through it with family, faith and hard work, and tell the men at church to look after each other. He wouldn't want government taking over, though he can't see who else could act fast.
S2.think: He'd be more frightened than he'd admit: a barely qualified apprentice who uses no technology, with his roofing fallback also going to robots. The yard money is for the kids, not for him sitting at home.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essentials at once, including the holiday and a new truck, and leaves the yard money untouched as long as he can. Keeps going to work daily, and asks his farming brother-in-law about work and the pastor about church help for families.
S2.feel: Frightened, like the ground going soft under a ladder, and praying a lot.
S2.quote: Like the ground's gone soft under the ladder. I'd pray a lot, honestly.
S2.fieldNote: His public calm and private fear are far apart in this scenario. When I named his contradiction about government, he admitted he'd hold his nose and accept it. His supports are family and church, and he'd keep turning up to work out of pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get your house in order, and I'd say it from the touchline to anyone who'd listen. Pay your debts, help your neighbour, teach your kids to work. I'd not be shouting about AI, I'd be talking about families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gets me qualified and a few years of good wages, which counts for something. But I'd be 48 with nothing to fall back on but roofs, and the robots are coming for roofs too. I don't see myself learning computers, I'm too set in my ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, take every bit of overtime and storm work, and put it all towards paying off the mortgage. I'd start doing small roofing repairs on Saturdays for people from church, cash in hand, to keep my hand in and bring a bit extra. And I'd keep the yard money safe, no shares, no gambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Five years is enough to get a roof on before the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots are coming for roofs too. Why go back to roofing on Saturdays, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's what I know, and for a few years at least people will want someone they trust on their roof. It's not a plan for forever. It's a way to keep the money coming in while the rest of the world sorts itself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ben, who'd be nineteen by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him what my dad told me: learn a trade, work hard, look after your family. Maybe that's out of date by then, I honestly don't know. But I don't know what else to tell him.

S3.say: He'd say five years is time to get your house in order: pay debts, help neighbours and teach kids to work. He'd talk about families rather than AI.
S3.think: He thinks five years buys a qualification and good wages, but at 48 he'd only have roofing to fall back on, and robots would reach roofs too. He doesn't see himself learning computers.
S3.do: Qualifies and takes all the overtime and storm work to pay off the mortgage. Does small cash roofing repairs on Saturdays for church members, and keeps the yard money safe from shares or risk.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, with time to get a roof on before the rain.
S3.quote: I'd tell him what my dad told me: learn a trade, work hard, look after your family. Maybe that's out of date by then, I honestly don't know.
S3.fieldNote: Marco admits his advice to his son may be out of date and has nothing to replace it. His Saturday roofing is a stopgap, and he knows it. He'd use five years to clear debt rather than to change himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, and a lot can change, including whether it happens at all. I'd tell people to keep working, keep praying, and keep their families close. I'd not lose sleep in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means a decent run as a lineworker, the mortgage gone, and the kids grown. I'd be 53, and with the yard money we'd be fine even if I never worked again, though I'd hate that. It's far enough away that I can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work hard, and pay off the mortgage within about six years. I'd keep the Saturday roofing going. And I'd push Ben towards an apprenticeship in something that needs a man on site, and talk to Lucy about nursing or teaching, things where people need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Ten years is a long time in a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate never working again, even if you could afford it. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a man who doesn't work goes soft, in the body and the head. My dad retired and he was in the garden every day until the end, fixing fences that didn't need fixing. I'd be the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you think about learning any of the new technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, once I see it working on our crew. If Walt starts using it, I'll take a look. If Walt doesn't, I won't.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long way off and might not even happen, and tell people to keep working, praying and keeping their families close. He wouldn't show worry in public.
S4.think: He thinks ten years means a good run as a lineworker, no mortgage and grown kids. At 53, the yard money means they'd be fine even if he never worked again, though he'd hate that.
S4.do: Qualifies, works hard and aims to clear the mortgage in about six years while keeping Saturday roofing going. Steers Ben towards an on-site apprenticeship and Lucy towards nursing or teaching.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, because ten years is a long time in a family.
S4.quote: My dad retired and he was in the garden every day until the end, fixing fences that didn't need fixing.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, his money worry fades and what's left is fear of idleness. He'd only try new technology if his crew leader did first. His plans run through family and on-site trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the speed of it, before I've even qualified, and with nothing to fall back on. What would help is the company keeping on the men it's already trained for as long as it can, and churches and families pulling together, and maybe, I'd hate to say it, some help from the government to stop things falling apart while people find their feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and for me that's the big one. Whatever happens with machines, I believe a man's worth isn't what he earns. I'd need to hold onto that pretty hard in the fast one.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with machines, I believe a man's worth isn't what he earns.
portrait: Marco Zhang is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice on a rural line crew, after eighteen years running a roofing firm with his father, whose yard sale left the family comfortable. He's a churchgoing football coach who never uses AI and trusts the experience of his crew leader Walt over any machine. Calm in the plateau and steady change, where his complaint is pride rather than fear, he becomes alarmed when AGI arrives in two years and he'd have no trade and no fallback. With more time he pays down the mortgage, does Saturday roofing for church members and leans on family and faith, while admitting the advice his father gave him may be out of date.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because of the speed: he wouldn't even be qualified and would have nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping on the workers it has trained, churches and families pulling together, and, reluctantly, some government help to keep things from falling apart.
